questions.question: Define a settlement, state the true dividing line between rural and urban settlements, and distinguish site from situation with one example of each.
questions.expected_answer: A settlement is any place where people live, together with the buildings and structures they use — from a single farmstead to a metropolis. The rural–urban dividing line is dominant economic activity, not size: rural settlements live mainly off primary activities (farming, forestry, fishing, mining), urban ones off secondary and tertiary activities. Site is the physical character of the exact ground the settlement stands on — relief, drainage, soil, water, aspect — for example a village on a well-drained, north-facing slope beside a spring. Situation is the settlement's position relative to its surroundings — routes, rivers, other settlements — for example a town where two national roads meet, midway between two cities. Site is under the settlement; situation is around it.

questions.question: Contrast dispersed and nucleated rural settlement patterns and give the underlying reason for each.
questions.expected_answer: Dispersed settlement scatters individual homesteads far apart, each on its own land, as in commercial wheat or maize districts; the reason is large, privately owned farms on which the farmer must live. Nucleated settlement clusters dwellings tightly around a central point — a water source, church or kraal — with the farmland around the outside, as in many villages on communal land; the reasons are communal land tenure, defence, shared water and community life. The pattern-to-ownership link is the key: scattered goes with private land, clustered with shared land.

questions.question: Name the four rural village shapes with the cause behind each, and list the three land-use functions of rural settlements with a South African example of each.
questions.expected_answer: Round village: dwellings ring a central open space or cattle kraal — built for defence and community life. Linear village: buildings strung one or two deep along a road, river or ridge foot — caused by the demand for frontage on the routeway. T-shaped village: buildings along both arms where a side road ends against a main road; crossroad village: buildings along all four arms where two roads cross — both caused by junction trade where traffic slows and stops. Functions: farming — crop farming such as Swartland wheat or KwaZulu-Natal coastal sugar, and stock farming such as Karoo sheep, with intensive farming supporting denser settlement and extensive farming spreading homesteads far apart; forestry — plantation villages and sawmill settlements in the escarpment and midlands timber country; conservation — staff villages, rest camps and gate settlements serving parks such as Addo Elephant National Park.
